name: Ondansetron
route_note: Oral tablets, orally disintegrating tablets, film or solution; IV or IM injection; suppositories in some countries

discovery.note: A carbazolone 5-HT3 antagonist selected after the role of serotonin in cisplatin-induced emesis was recognised.

tagline: First 5-HT3 antagonist, a mainstay for chemotherapy and postoperative nausea
summary: Ondansetron blocks serotonin 5-HT3 receptors and was the first drug of its class. It revolutionised prevention of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting and is widely used for postoperative and radiotherapy-induced nausea.
mechanism: Chemotherapy and radiation damage enterochromaffin cells in the gut, releasing serotonin, which activates 5-HT3 receptors on vagal afferent nerves and triggers vomiting via the brainstem.

Ondansetron blocks 5-HT3 receptors both peripherally on vagal terminals and centrally in the chemoreceptor trigger zone and nucleus tractus solitarius. It has no meaningful dopamine-blocking action, so it lacks extrapyramidal effects.
uses: Prevention of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting
Prevention of radiotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting
Prevention and treatment of postoperative nausea and vomiting

serious: QT prolongation and torsades de pointes
Serotonin syndrome with other serotonergic drugs

facts: Ondansetron was one of several major drugs, with salbutamol and ranitidine, to come from David Jack's Glaxo research group.
It is often combined with dexamethasone and an NK1 antagonist such as aprepitant for highly emetogenic chemotherapy.
